CHAPTER II.


Mrs. John Dashwood now installed herself mistress of Norland; and her
mother and sisters-in-law were degraded to the condition of visitors.
As such, however, they were treated by her with quiet civility; and by
her husband with as much kindness as he could feel towards anybody
beyond himself, his wife, and their child. He really pressed them, with
some earnestness, to consider Norland as their home; and, as no plan
appeared so eligible to Mrs. Dashwood as remaining there till she could
accommodate herself with a house in the neighbourhood, his invitation
was accepted.

A continuance in a place where everything reminded her of former
delight, was exactly what suited her mind. In seasons of cheerfulness,
no temper could be more cheerful than hers, or possess, in a greater
degree, that sanguine expectation of happiness which is happiness
itself. But in sorrow she must be equally carried away by her fancy,
and as far beyond consolation as in pleasure she was beyond alloy.

Mrs. John Dashwood did not at all approve of what her husband intended
to do for his sisters. To take three thousand pounds from the fortune
of their dear little boy would be impoverishing him to the most
dreadful degree. She begged him to think again on the subject. How
could he answer it to himself to rob his child, and his only child too,
of so large a sum? And what possible claim could the Miss Dashwoods,
who were related to him only by half blood, which she considered as no
relationship at all, have on his generosity to so large an amount. It
was very well known that no affection was ever supposed to exist
between the children of any man by different marriages; and why was he
to ruin himself, and their poor little Harry, by giving away all his
money to his half sisters?

“It was my father’s last request to me,” replied her husband, “that I
should assist his widow and daughters.”

“He did not know what he was talking of, I dare say; ten to one but he
was light-headed at the time. Had he been in his right senses, he could
not have thought of such a thing as begging you to give away half your
fortune from your own child.”

“He did not stipulate for any particular sum, my dear Fanny; he only
requested me, in general terms, to assist them, and make their
situation more comfortable than it was in his power to do. Perhaps it
would have been as well if he had left it wholly to myself. He could
hardly suppose I should neglect them. But as he required the promise, I
could not do less than give it; at least I thought so at the time. The
promise, therefore, was given, and must be performed. Something must be
done for them whenever they leave Norland and settle in a new home.”

“Well, then, _let_ something be done for them; but _that_ something
need not be three thousand pounds. Consider,” she added, “that when the
money is once parted with, it never can return. Your sisters will
marry, and it will be gone for ever. If, indeed, it could be restored
to our poor little boy—”

“Why, to be sure,” said her husband, very gravely, “that would make
great difference. The time may come when Harry will regret that so
large a sum was parted with. If he should have a numerous family, for
instance, it would be a very convenient addition.”

“To be sure it would.”

“Perhaps, then, it would be better for all parties, if the sum were
diminished one half.—Five hundred pounds would be a prodigious increase
to their fortunes!”

“Oh! beyond anything great! What brother on earth would do half so much
for his sisters, even if _really_ his sisters! And as it is—only half
blood!—But you have such a generous spirit!”

“I would not wish to do any thing mean,” he replied. “One had rather,
on such occasions, do too much than too little. No one, at least, can
think I have not done enough for them: even themselves, they can hardly
expect more.”

“There is no knowing what _they_ may expect,” said the lady, “but we
are not to think of their expectations: the question is, what you can
afford to do.”

“Certainly—and I think I may afford to give them five hundred pounds
a-piece. As it is, without any addition of mine, they will each have
about three thousand pounds on their mother’s death—a very comfortable
fortune for any young woman.”

“To be sure it is; and, indeed, it strikes me that they can want no
addition at all. They will have ten thousand pounds divided amongst
them. If they marry, they will be sure of doing well, and if they do
not, they may all live very comfortably together on the interest of ten
thousand pounds.”

“That is very true, and, therefore, I do not know whether, upon the
whole, it would not be more advisable to do something for their mother
while she lives, rather than for them—something of the annuity kind I
mean.—My sisters would feel the good effects of it as well as herself.
A hundred a year would make them all perfectly comfortable.”

His wife hesitated a little, however, in giving her consent to this
plan.

“To be sure,” said she, “it is better than parting with fifteen hundred
pounds at once. But, then, if Mrs. Dashwood should live fifteen years
we shall be completely taken in.”

“Fifteen years! my dear Fanny; her life cannot be worth half that
purchase.”

“Certainly not; but if you observe, people always live for ever when
there is an annuity to be paid them; and she is very stout and healthy,
and hardly forty. An annuity is a very serious business; it comes over
and over every year, and there is no getting rid of it. You are not
aware of what you are doing. I have known a great deal of the trouble
of annuities; for my mother was clogged with the payment of three to
old superannuated servants by my father’s will, and it is amazing how
disagreeable she found it. Twice every year these annuities were to be
paid; and then there was the trouble of getting it to them; and then
one of them was said to have died, and afterwards it turned out to be
no such thing. My mother was quite sick of it. Her income was not her
own, she said, with such perpetual claims on it; and it was the more
unkind in my father, because, otherwise, the money would have been
entirely at my mother’s disposal, without any restriction whatever. It
has given me such an abhorrence of annuities, that I am sure I would
not pin myself down to the payment of one for all the world.”

“It is certainly an unpleasant thing,” replied Mr. Dashwood, “to have
those kind of yearly drains on one’s income. One’s fortune, as your
mother justly says, is _not_ one’s own. To be tied down to the regular
payment of such a sum, on every rent day, is by no means desirable: it
takes away one’s independence.”

“Undoubtedly; and after all you have no thanks for it. They think
themselves secure, you do no more than what is expected, and it raises
no gratitude at all. If I were you, whatever I did should be done at my
own discretion entirely. I would not bind myself to allow them any
thing yearly. It may be very inconvenient some years to spare a
hundred, or even fifty pounds from our own expenses.”

“I believe you are right, my love; it will be better that there should
be no annuity in the case; whatever I may give them occasionally will
be of far greater assistance than a yearly allowance, because they
would only enlarge their style of living if they felt sure of a larger
income, and would not be sixpence the richer for it at the end of the
year. It will certainly be much the best way. A present of fifty
pounds, now and then, will prevent their ever being distressed for
money, and will, I think, be amply discharging my promise to my
father.”

“To be sure it will. Indeed, to say the truth, I am convinced within
myself that your father had no idea of your giving them any money at
all. The assistance he thought of, I dare say, was only such as might
be reasonably expected of you; for instance, such as looking out for a
comfortable small house for them, helping them to move their things,
and sending them presents of fish and game, and so forth, whenever they
are in season. I’ll lay my life that he meant nothing farther; indeed,
it would be very strange and unreasonable if he did. Do but consider,
my dear Mr. Dashwood, how excessively comfortable your mother-in-law
and her daughters may live on the interest of seven thousand pounds,
besides the thousand pounds belonging to each of the girls, which
brings them in fifty pounds a year a-piece, and, of course, they will
pay their mother for their board out of it. Altogether, they will have
five hundred a-year amongst them, and what on earth can four women want
for more than that?—They will live so cheap! Their housekeeping will be
nothing at all. They will have no carriage, no horses, and hardly any
servants; they will keep no company, and can have no expenses of any
kind! Only conceive how comfortable they will be! Five hundred a year!
I am sure I cannot imagine how they will spend half of it; and as to
your giving them more, it is quite absurd to think of it. They will be
much more able to give _you_ something.”

“Upon my word,” said Mr. Dashwood, “I believe you are perfectly right.
My father certainly could mean nothing more by his request to me than
what you say. I clearly understand it now, and I will strictly fulfil
my engagement by such acts of assistance and kindness to them as you
have described. When my mother removes into another house my services
shall be readily given to accommodate her as far as I can. Some little
present of furniture too may be acceptable then.”

“Certainly,” returned Mrs. John Dashwood. “But, however, _one_ thing
must be considered. When your father and mother moved to Norland,
though the furniture of Stanhill was sold, all the china, plate, and
linen was saved, and is now left to your mother. Her house will
therefore be almost completely fitted up as soon as she takes it.”

“That is a material consideration undoubtedly. A valuable legacy
indeed! And yet some of the plate would have been a very pleasant
addition to our own stock here.”

“Yes; and the set of breakfast china is twice as handsome as what
belongs to this house. A great deal too handsome, in my opinion, for
any place _they_ can ever afford to live in. But, however, so it is.
Your father thought only of _them_. And I must say this: that you owe
no particular gratitude to him, nor attention to his wishes; for we
very well know that if he could, he would have left almost everything
in the world to _them_.”

This argument was irresistible. It gave to his intentions whatever of
decision was wanting before; and he finally resolved, that it would be
absolutely unnecessary, if not highly indecorous, to do more for the
widow and children of his father, than such kind of neighbourly acts as
his own wife pointed out.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER I. OUTSIDE

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’

The door slammed with the dull, decisive thud of bureaucratic finality.

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.

It was a ground-floor sash, thrown wide to the deluge. I had only to breach the perimeter to secure dry cover. There was no watch, no patrol, no sign of life in the immediate vicinity. Out here, I was at the mercy of the elements, another anonymous casualty waiting to be swept into the Thames. The tramp at the casual ward had surrendered his freedom to the constabulary in exchange for a warm cell. I preferred to maintain my operational independence.

Perhaps the villa was empty. Civilian carelessness was a luxury of the secure and the comfortable. I considered knocking to alert the occupants of their vulnerability, perhaps angling for a meager reward. But experience in a harder school had taught me the futility of relying on the gratitude of the comfortable classes. More likely, I would be turned over to the authorities as a vagrant. Better to appropriate the shelter and vanish before dawn.

I leaned over the low brick wall, testing the air. The thermal differential was immediate; warmth bled from the dark aperture. Moving with deliberate silence, I vaulted the barrier. The ground beneath my boots felt cemented and stable. I pressed myself against the exterior masonry, listening at the crevice. Complete silence. Conversely, in sorrow, she was equally susceptible to her imagination, retreating into fantasies that placed her far beyond the reach of consolation, just as her pleasure often transcended mere alloy.

However, Mrs. John Dashwood harbored a profound objection to her husband's intention regarding his sisters. To strip three thousand pounds from the inheritance of their beloved young son would be to reduce him to destitution. She implored him to reconsider, asking how he could justify robbing his only child of such a substantial sum. Furthermore, what moral claim did the Miss Dashwoods hold? They were connected to him solely by half-blood, a distinction she regarded as non-existent. Society universally acknowledged that no affection existed between children born of different marriages; thus, why should he ruin himself and their poor little Harry by squandering his wealth on these half-sisters?

"It was my father's last request," her husband replied firmly. "That I should assist his widow and daughters."

"He was likely light-headed at the time," she countered sharply. "Ten to one he lacked his faculties. Had he been in his right senses, he could not have conceived of begging you to give away half your fortune from your own child."

"He made no specific stipulation for a sum, my dear Fanny," he corrected gently. "Only a general request to assist them and improve their circumstances. Perhaps it would have been wiser if he had left the matter entirely to my discretion. He could hardly have imagined I would neglect them. But since he demanded a promise, I felt bound to give it. At least, that was my reasoning at the time. The promise stands and must be fulfilled. Something must be arranged for them once they depart Norland."

"Very well, then," she conceded reluctantly. "_Let_ something be done. But that 'something' need not amount to three thousand pounds. Consider," she added, her voice tightening, "once money leaves your possession, it never returns. Your sisters will marry, and it will be gone forever. If, indeed, it could be restored to our poor little boy—"

"Why, to be sure," her husband said gravely, "that would alter the equation significantly. The day may come when Harry regrets parting with such a large sum. Should he establish a numerous family, for instance, it would serve as a remarkably convenient addition to his resources."

"To be sure, it would."

"Perhaps, then, reducing the sum by half would benefit all parties. Five hundred pounds would constitute a prodigious increase to their fortunes!"

"Oh! Beyond anything great! What brother on earth would offer half so much to his sisters, even if they were truly his sisters? And as it is—they are only half-blood!—But you possess such a generous spirit!"

"I would not wish to act meanly," he replied. "On such occasions, one errs more by doing too little than too much. No one, at least, can accuse me of insufficient effort; indeed, they could hardly expect more."

"There is no knowing what _they_ may expect," the lady interjected, "but we must disregard their expectations. The question remains: what can you afford?"

"Certainly. I believe I can afford to give them five hundred pounds apiece. Without my contribution, they will each inherit approximately three thousand pounds upon their mother's death—a very comfortable fortune for any young woman."

"To be sure it is. Indeed, it strikes me they require no further augmentation. With ten thousand pounds divided among them, they are assured of success if they marry, or a life of comfort if they remain single, living off the interest."

"That is accurate. Therefore, I fail to see why it would not be more prudent to provide for their mother during her lifetime rather than for the daughters. I refer to an annuity. My sisters would feel the benefits as acutely as she would. A hundred pounds annually would render them all perfectly content."

Mrs. Dashwood hesitated slightly before consenting to this proposal. "Admittedly," she said, "it is preferable to parting with fifteen hundred pounds outright. However, if Mrs. Dashwood survives fifteen years, we shall be thoroughly deceived."

"Fifteen years! My dear Fanny, her life cannot be valued at half that price."

"Certainly not; yet, observe, people invariably live indefinitely when an annuity is involved. She is robust, healthy, and hardly forty. An annuity is a binding commitment; it recurs annually and offers no escape. You are unaware of the entanglement you invite. I have witnessed the turmoil surrounding annuities firsthand. My mother was burdened by payments to three elderly servants mandated by my father's will. It was astonishing how disagreeable it became. Twice yearly, funds had to be disbursed, accompanied by the logistical nightmare of delivery. Then came the false reports of death, later proven untrue. My mother grew utterly sick of it. She claimed her income was no longer her own, shackled by perpetual demands. It was particularly cruel, considering the money would have been entirely at her disposal without restriction. I harbor such an abhorrence of annuities that I would not agree to one under any circumstance."

"It is certainly an unpleasant mechanism," Mr. Dashwood admitted. "Those yearly drains on one's income are vexatious. As your mother rightly noted, a fortune is not truly one's own. Being tethered to the rigid obligation of such payments on every rent day strips away one's independence."

"Undoubtedly. Moreover, you receive no gratitude. They assume security; you perform merely the duty expected of you, eliciting no appreciation. If I were you, I would exercise complete discretion. I would not bind myself to annual allowances. It may prove inconvenient in lean years to spare a hundred, or even fifty pounds from our own expenses."

"I believe you are right, my love. It is superior to establish no annuity. Any occasional gift will offer far greater assistance than a fixed allowance, as they might simply elevate their lifestyle if assured of increased income, gaining no net wealth by year's end. It is undoubtedly the optimal path. Occasional gifts of fifty pounds will prevent distress and, I trust, adequately discharge my promise to my father."

"To be sure it will. Frankly, I am convinced your father never envisioned you providing monetary aid. The assistance he contemplated was likely reasonable social support: securing a modest dwelling, aiding their relocation, and sending seasonal provisions like fish and game. I wager my life he meant nothing more. It would be bizarre and unreasonable to expect financial ruin. Consider, my dear Mr. Dashwood, how comfortably your mother-in-law and her daughters can subsist on the interest of seven thousand pounds, plus the five hundred pounds generated by the individual legacies of the girls. They will effectively pay their mother for board from this sum. Altogether, they command five hundred pounds annually. What on earth can four women desire beyond that? They will live frugally. Housekeeping costs will be negligible. They will own no carriages, no horses, and employ minimal servants. They will avoid society and incur no expenses whatsoever. Conceive the comfort of five hundred pounds a year! I cannot imagine how they would spend half of it. Regarding any further provision from you, it is absurd. They will be far more capable of offering _you_ something."

"Upon my word," Mr. Dashwood conceded, "I believe you are entirely correct. My father surely meant nothing more than you suggest. I now clearly comprehend his intent, and I shall strictly fulfill my engagement through the acts of assistance and kindness you have outlined. When your mother relocates, my services will be freely offered to facilitate her transition. A modest donation of furniture may also prove acceptable."

"Certainly," Mrs. John Dashwood agreed. "However, one critical factor must be weighed. When your parents moved to Norland, although the Stanhill furniture was sold, all the china, plate, and linen were preserved and now belong to your mother. Consequently, her new home will be nearly fully furnished upon her arrival."

"This is a material consideration, undoubtedly. A valuable legacy indeed! And yet, some of the silverware would have been a delightful addition to our own stock here."

"Yes; and the breakfast service is twice as exquisite as ours. Far too handsome, in my opinion, for any establishment they can realistically afford. Nevertheless, so it is. Your father thought only of _them_. I must add this: you owe him neither particular gratitude nor strict adherence to his wishes. We know full well that if he possessed the ability, he would have bequeathed almost everything in the world to _them_."

This argument proved irresistible. It supplied the necessary resolve to his wavering intentions. He finally concluded that it would be not only unnecessary but highly indecorous to provide the widow and children of his father with more than the neighborly gestures his wife had suggested.
